pos: n. (the Rouergue see whose town was split by a wall between the bishop's city and the count's burg)
etymology: From the Gaulish tribe the Ruteni, through Latin Rutenis; the province took the name Rouergue.
biblical_def: Rodez in the Rouergue was a see from the fifth century, and for much of the Middle Ages the town was literally divided. The bishop held the Cite around the cathedral and the count of Rodez held the Bourg, each with its own walls, consuls, courts and militia, and a wall between them; the two quarters quarrelled, fortified against each other, and were not finally united until the sixteenth century. The cathedral of Notre-Dame, built of red sandstone with a great sixteenth-century bell tower, formed part of the city's defences, its west front built blind into the rampart. The dictionary records Rodez for the dividing wall, because a bishop who needs a wall against the count has accepted a definition of his office that Scripture does not supply. The New Testament overseer is given a flock and not a quarter: “Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock” (Act 20:28), and his weapon is named, “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph 6:17), which is a text. “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6) settles what he may not reach for.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a citadel as a fortress in a city; a consul as a chief magistrate; a rampart as a mound of earth round a place; jurisdiction as legal authority; and a flock as a company of the faithful.
webster_full: CITADEL, n. A fortress or castle in or near a city, intended for its defense.
CONSUL, n. In Roman history, the chief magistrate of the commonwealth; in some free cities, a chief magistrate.
RAMPART, n. In fortification, an elevation or mound of earth round a place, capable of resisting the cannon of an enemy.
JURISDICTION, n. The legal power or authority of doing justice in cases of complaint; the power of executing the laws.
FLOCK, n. A company or collection; applied to sheep and other small animals; a Christian church.

corruption_summary: Rouergue see whose town was split by a wall between the bishop's city and the count's burg, each fortified against the other.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the content of the overseer's charge. Paul hands the Ephesian elders a flock, “Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock” (Act 20:28), and hands the Christian one weapon, “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph 6:17), which is the word of God and not a militia.

The live temptation is to think a bishop needs temporal footing to protect his people. Zechariah forecloses it for any work of God, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6), and Malachi gives the office its actual description, “he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts” (Mal 2:7) — a man whose lips keep knowledge, with no quarter to garrison.

pos: n. (the Gevaudan see in the Cevennes, whose bishop was count of Gevaudan)
etymology: From Latin Mimate, of uncertain Gaulish origin; the Occitan form is Mende.
biblical_def: Mende lies high in the Lot valley on the edge of the Cevennes, the see of the Gevaudan, whose bishops held the county as well and ruled the district as temporal lords under an agreement with the French crown of 1307. The cathedral was begun in 1368 at the expense of Urban V, a pope born a few miles away at Grizac, and it carried one of the largest bells in Christendom until the Huguenots destroyed the church in 1579, leaving only the towers; it was rebuilt in the following century. The surrounding Cevennes were the heartland of the Camisard resistance after the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes. The dictionary records Mende for its position between those two facts: a bishop-count's cathedral in a country that became the most stubbornly Protestant in France. Both the destruction of 1579 and the dragonnades that followed 1685 fail the same test, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6), and the faith the Cevenol peasants held in caves rested where everyone's must, on “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8) and “I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation” (Rom 1:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a dragonnade is given under dragoon as a soldier who serves on foot or horseback; a Huguenot as a French protestant; persecution as the infliction of pain for religion; a conventicle as a secret assembly for worship; and constancy as firmness of mind.
webster_full: DRAGOON, n. A soldier or musketeer who serves on horseback or on foot, as occasion may require.
HUGUENOT, n. A name given by way of contempt to the French protestants.
PERSECUTION, n. The infliction of pain, punishment or death upon others unjustly, particularly for adhering to a religious creed.
CONVENTICLE, n. An assembly or meeting; usually, a meeting of dissenters from the established church, for religious worship.
CONSTANCY, n. Fixedness; a standing firm; firmness of mind; stability in attachments.

corruption_summary: Gevaudan see whose bishops were also counts, its cathedral destroyed by Huguenots in 1579, in a district that became Camisard country.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the test does not change with the side holding the weapon. Huguenots pulled down Mende's cathedral in 1579 and dragoons harried the Cevennes after 1685, and “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6) condemns both without distinction.

The live temptation is to let sympathy settle the doctrine, so that the persecuted are presumed sound. The Cevenol peasants were largely sound, but not because they suffered; their standing rested where all does, “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8). What they held onto was a gospel, “I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation” (Rom 1:16), and a deposit worth the fight, “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3).

pos: n. (the Flemish cloth town and see whose bishop Cornelius Jansen gave his name to Jansenism)
etymology: From the river Ieper or the elm, Flemish Ieper; the French form Ypres is the one English uses.
biblical_def: Ypres in Flanders was one of the three great cloth towns of the medieval Low Countries, and its Cloth Hall was among the largest commercial buildings in Europe before it was destroyed in the First World War and rebuilt. A bishopric was created there in 1559 in Philip II's reorganisation of the Netherlands sees, and its second bishop was Cornelius Jansen, consecrated in 1636 and dead of plague in 1638. His Augustinus, published posthumously in 1640, set out Augustine's doctrine of grace — the bondage of the will, efficacious grace, predestination — and gave its name to the Jansenist movement that Rome condemned in 1653 and crushed over the following century. The dictionary records Ypres for Jansen, who is the most interesting figure in post-Tridentine Catholicism from a Reformed point of view. He read Augustine correctly on grace and tried to hold the result inside a church whose council had already excluded it. “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8) and “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) are what he found, and “a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28) is the step he would not take.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Jansenism as the doctrine of Jansenius concerning grace and predestination; efficacious as producing effects; predestination as the decree of God; a bull as a papal letter; and bondage as slavery.
webster_full: JANSENISM, n. The doctrine of Jansenius, in regard to free will and grace.
EFFICACIOUS, a. That has power adequate to the purpose intended; powerful in effect.
PREDESTINATION, n. The act of decreeing or foreordaining events; the purpose of God from eternity respecting all events.
BULL, n. A letter, edict or rescript of the pope, published or transmitted to the churches.
BONDAGE, n. Slavery or involuntary servitude; captivity; imprisonment; restraint of a person's liberty.

corruption_summary: Flemish cloth town and see whose bishop Cornelius Jansen wrote the Augustinus, published 1640, from which Jansenism took its name.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Jansen read Augustine right. The bondage of the will and the efficacy of grace are Augustine's and Paul's before they are anybody's party doctrine: “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8), guarded by “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9).

The live temptation is to claim Jansen as a Protestant, which he refused to be, or to dismiss him as a sectarian, which he was not. He stopped one step short. The sentence he would not finally stand on alone is “a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28), stated negatively as “a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ” (Gal 2:16), and a church that has anathematised that clause cannot house the doctrine of grace that produces it.

pos: n. (the prince-bishopric on the Meuse, an independent state within the Empire until 1795)
etymology: From Latin Leodium, of Frankish origin; the Dutch form is Luik and the German Luttich.
biblical_def: Liege on the Meuse was for eight hundred years not merely a see but a state. From the early eleventh century its bishops held the rank of prince of the Holy Roman Empire and governed a territory straddling the Meuse with its own laws, coinage, army and diplomacy, surviving as an independent principality until the French annexation of 1795. The city had a strong tradition of communal liberties, repeatedly in arms against its own bishop, and the Peace of Fexhe in 1316 set limits on his power that are sometimes called an early constitution. Liege was also a centre of metalwork and, later, of coal and arms manufacture. The dictionary records Liege as the clearest European instance of the bishop as sovereign, which is the arrangement the Reformation attacked at its root. The two offices answer to different warrants and use different instruments. “Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock” (Act 20:28) is the bishop's whole commission, “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph 6:17) his only weapon, and “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6) the standing prohibition on confusing the two.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a principality as the territory of a prince; sovereignty as supreme power; a commune is given under commonalty as the common people; coinage as the act of coining money; and investiture as the giving of possession of an office.
webster_full: PRINCIPALITY, n. Sovereignty; supreme power; a prince; the territory of a prince, or the country which gives title to a prince.
SOVEREIGNTY, n. Supreme power; supremacy; the possession of the highest power, or of uncontrollable power.
COMMONALTY, n. The common people; the bulk of mankind; those below the rank of nobility.
COINAGE, n. The act, art or practice of stamping money; the charges or expense of coining money.
INVESTITURE, n. The act of giving possession of a manor, office or benefice.

corruption_summary: Prince-bishopric on the Meuse that governed itself as an independent state within the Empire until the French annexation of 1795.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the two offices are not combinable. Paul describes a bishop's work exhaustively, “Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock” (Act 20:28), and the believer's armoury contains one offensive weapon, “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph 6:17). A prince needs instruments a shepherd is never issued.

The live temptation is to credit Liege's communal liberties to episcopal government, when they were largely won against it. The governing prohibition is Zechariah's, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6), and the office's true dignity is Malachi's, “he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts” (Mal 2:7), which no coinage improves.

pos: n. (the see created in 1559 at the confluence of the Sambre and Meuse, under its great citadel)
etymology: From a Celtic root, perhaps namu, with Latin Namurcum; the Dutch form is Namen.
biblical_def: Namur stands where the Sambre joins the Meuse beneath a rock that has been fortified continuously since antiquity; its citadel was rebuilt by Vauban after the siege of 1692 and again in the nineteenth century, and the town was besieged in most European wars from the seventeenth century to the twentieth. A bishopric was erected there in 1559 as part of Philip II's reorganisation of the Netherlands dioceses, a scheme designed to tighten control over a region where Reformed preaching was spreading and which contributed directly to the revolt of 1566. The dictionary records Namur for the reason the see was created. It was an administrative answer to a doctrinal movement, and that is a category error the Reformation exposed everywhere. Reorganising dioceses cannot address what preaching has started, because the mechanism is not administrative: “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17), and the instrument is a text, “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph 6:17). “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11) is why the policy failed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a diocese as a bishop's jurisdiction; a citadel as a fortress in a city; a siege as the besetting of a fortified place; a revolt as a renunciation of allegiance; and reorganisation is given under organise as to form with suitable parts.
webster_full: DIOCESE, n. The circuit or extent of a bishop's jurisdiction; an ecclesiastical division of a kingdom.
CITADEL, n. A fortress or castle in or near a city, intended for its defense.
SIEGE, n. The setting of an army around or before a fortified place for the purpose of compelling the garrison to surrender.
REVOLT, n. Desertion; change of sides; a renunciation of allegiance and subjection to one's prince or state.
ORGANIZE, v.t. To construct so that one part may cooperate with another; to form with suitable organs.

corruption_summary: See erected in 1559 in Philip II's reorganisation of the Netherlands dioceses, an administrative response to the spread of Reformed preaching.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that preaching is not answered by administration. The 1559 scheme redrew boundaries against a movement whose mechanism Paul states plainly: “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17). You cannot redistrict a sentence out of a man's hearing.

The live temptation is to treat church structure as the decisive front, which both sides have done at various times. The instrument that was actually loose in the Netherlands is named, “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph 6:17), a text in people's hands, and Isaiah explains the outcome: “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11). The duty on either side of it is “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2).

pos: n. (Malines, the archbishopric made primatial see of the Low Countries in 1559)
etymology: From a Germanic root mahal, a place of assembly or judgment; the French form is Malines.
biblical_def: Mechelen, Malines in French, lies between Brussels and Antwerp and was the administrative capital of the Burgundian and Habsburg Netherlands: the Great Council, the supreme court of the provinces, sat there from 1473, and Margaret of Austria governed from it as regent in the early sixteenth century. In 1559 it was made an archbishopric and the primatial see of the whole Netherlands, its first archbishop being Antoine Perrenot de Granvelle. Its cathedral tower, left unfinished, still carries one of the great carillons. The dictionary records Mechelen for the primacy of 1559, which is the summit of the reorganisation that also created Ypres and Namur. The design was to supervise doctrine through a tightened hierarchy. What it met was something no hierarchy supervises: congregations reading. “searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11) describes that exactly, and once it is happening the ordinary machinery of oversight is beside the point, because the standard appealed to is “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) and the duty is laid on every hearer, “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a primate as a chief ecclesiastic; a carillon is given under chime as the harmony of bells; a regent as one who governs a kingdom in the minority of the king; a council as an assembly for deliberation; and hierarchy as an ecclesiastical government.
webster_full: PRIMATE, n. The chief ecclesiastic in the church; an archbishop who has jurisdiction over other bishops.
CHIME, n. The consonant or harmonic sounds of several correspondent instruments; a set of bells which are struck by hammers.
REGENT, n. One invested with vicarious authority; one who governs a kingdom in the minority or disability of the king.
COUNCIL, n. An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice.
HIERARCHY, n. An ecclesiastical establishment or government; a rank or order of sacred persons.

corruption_summary: Administrative capital of the Habsburg Netherlands, made archbishopric and primatial see in 1559 under Granvelle.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is where doctrinal authority actually sits. The 1559 primacy was built to supervise belief from above, and Luke praises a congregation that did the supervising itself: “searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11). The standard they used is the one Paul names, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16).

The live temptation is to think the dispute was about church polity first. It was about a text in the vernacular and a people reading it, which makes the duty general, “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21). The mechanism Paul describes runs below any hierarchy, “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17), which is why the reorganisation could not reach it.

pos: n. (Leuven, the Brabant university town whose faculty condemned Luther in 1519 and whose Trilingual College taught Hebrew and Greek)
etymology: From a Germanic form, perhaps Loven by the Dyle; the Dutch name is Leuven.
biblical_def: Louvain in Brabant received a university in 1425, the oldest in the Low Countries, and its theological faculty became the most authoritative in northern Europe. In November 1519 it issued, with Cologne, the first university condemnation of Luther's writings. Two years before, something quite different had been founded in the same town: the Collegium Trilingue, endowed by Jerome Busleyden and promoted by Erasmus, which taught Hebrew, Greek and Latin together and became a model for humanist biblical study across Europe. Louvain also produced the Louvain Bible of 1548 and the revised Vulgate work that fed the Sixto-Clementine edition. The dictionary records Louvain for holding those two things at once. The faculty that condemned Luther also taught the languages in which Luther's case was made, and the languages were the greater gift. “Study to shew thyself approved unto God” (2Ti 2:15) commands the work the Trilingue existed to do, and “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) is why the originals matter more than any faculty's verdict.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a faculty as the masters of a college; a humanist is given under humanity as grammatical studies; trilingual is given under lingual as pertaining to the tongue; a censure as a judicial sentence; and the originals as the first copies.
webster_full: FACULTY, n. The body of individuals constituting the instructors or officers of a college; one of the departments of learning.
HUMANITY, n. In the plural, grammatical studies, or the study of the Greek and Latin classics.
LINGUAL, a. Pertaining to the tongue; uttered by the aid of the tongue.
CENSURE, n. The act of blaming or finding fault and condemning as wrong; a judicial sentence.
ORIGINAL, n. First copy; archetype; that from which any thing is transcribed or translated.
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
corruption_summary: Brabant university town whose faculty issued the first academic condemnation of Luther in 1519, and whose Trilingual College of 1517 taught Hebrew, Greek and Latin.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the primacy of the original languages over any tribunal. Louvain condemned Luther and taught the Greek and Hebrew that made his argument answerable only from the text. Paul's command is “Study to shew thyself approved unto God” (2Ti 2:15), whose verb concerns cutting straight.

The live temptation is to treat a faculty's censure as settling a question. The claim of inspiration is made for the writings, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16), not for the commentators, and the examination belongs to the hearers, “searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11). Paul leaves the testing with the congregation, “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21), which is what 1519 declined to do.

pos: n. (the Swiss abbey and Black Madonna shrine where Zwingli served as people's priest from 1516)
etymology: German Einsiedeln, the hermitages, from Einsiedler, a hermit; founded at the cell of Meinrad.
biblical_def: Einsiedeln in Schwyz grew up at the hermitage of Meinrad, killed in 861, and became a Benedictine abbey with an exemption placing it directly under the Empire. Its Lady Chapel held a Black Madonna and drew one of the largest pilgrimages in Europe, promoted by a plenary indulgence attached to the shrine's dedication. From 1516 to the end of 1518 the people's priest at Einsiedeln was Huldrych Zwingli, and it was there, surrounded by the pilgrim traffic and reading Erasmus' Greek New Testament, that his preaching turned: he began to tell the crowds that Christ alone forgives and that the journey to the shrine gained them nothing. From Einsiedeln he went to the Grossmunster at Zurich in 1519. The dictionary records Einsiedeln as the place where the Swiss Reformation began in a man's mind, and the trigger was the gap between the traffic and the text. “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (Mat 11:28) is addressed to the labouring, “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.” (Joh 4:24) unfixes worship from the chapel, and “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) cancels the indulgence.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an indulgence as remission of penalty granted by the pope; a pilgrimage as a journey to a holy place; an image as a representation; intercession as prayer on behalf of another; and remission as forgiveness.
webster_full: INDULGENCE, n. In the Romish church, remission of the penalty due to sins, granted by the pope.
PILGRIMAGE, n. A journey which a person takes to visit some holy place, as to the sepulchre of Christ at Jerusalem.
IMAGE, n. A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance; a statue.
INTERCESSION, n. Prayer or solicitation to one party in favor of another.
REMISSION, n. Forgiveness; pardon; that is, the giving up of the punishment due to a crime.
scriptures: Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
Joh 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
corruption_summary: Swiss Benedictine abbey and Black Madonna pilgrimage shrine where Zwingli served from 1516 and began preaching against the pilgrimage itself.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what Zwingli saw at the shrine. Crowds had walked to a chapel for relief that Christ offers directly: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (Mat 11:28). The invitation names the labouring and the laden, which is precisely who was arriving at Einsiedeln.

The live temptation is to defend the pilgrimage as harmless popular devotion. It carried an indulgence, which makes it a transaction, and “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) voids it. Christ had already removed worship from any particular place, “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.” (Joh 4:24), and the whole of what the pilgrims wanted is given on other terms: “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8).

Greek pneuma (G4151) — spirit, breath; “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.”, John 4:24.
Greek ergon (G2041) — a work, a deed; “Not of works, lest any man should boast.”, Ephesians 2:9.

“God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.” (Joh 4:24) — worship unfixed from the chapel.

pos: n. (the Alsatian imperial abbey founded 727 by Pirmin, famed for its library)
etymology: German Murbach, the walled or boundary brook, from Mur and Bach.
biblical_def: Murbach in a wooded valley of the Vosges was founded in 727 by Pirmin, the missionary bishop who also founded Reichenau, with the endowment of Count Eberhard of Alsace. It became an imperial abbey of great wealth, its abbot a prince of the Empire, and it assembled one of the best libraries north of the Alps; the ninth-century Murbach catalogue survives and lists several hundred volumes, and Murbach manuscripts are now scattered through European collections. The abbey was secularised in 1789 and only the choir and transept of its Romanesque church remain. The dictionary records Murbach for the catalogue, which belongs with Buildwas' and Titchfield's. Three surviving book-lists from three countries show the same thing: the medieval church held Scripture in quantity, read it in Latin, and kept it among the few. “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) was true of every volume; “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.” (Psa 119:130) names the result it did not produce, because the benefit promised is to the simple and the shelves were not theirs.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a catalogue as a list disposed in order; secularisation is given under secularise as to convert from sacred to common use; an abbot as the superior of an abbey; a volume as a book; and the simple as the unlearned.
webster_full: CATALOGUE, n. A list or enumeration of the names of men or things disposed in a certain order.
SECULARIZE, v.t. To make secular; to convert from spiritual appropriation to secular or common use.
ABBOT, n. The superior or governor of an abbey or monastery.
VOLUME, n. A book; a collection of sheets of paper bound together.
SIMPLE, a. Artless; unaffected; sincere; weak in intellect; not wise or sagacious.
scriptures: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.
corruption_summary: Alsatian imperial abbey founded 727 by Pirmin, holder of one of the great northern libraries, with a ninth-century catalogue that survives.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that custody is not circulation. Murbach's catalogue proves a serious collection, and the apostolic claim covers it entirely, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16). But the Psalmist attaches the promise to an effect in people, “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.” (Psa 119:130), and names the beneficiaries as the simple.

The live temptation is to answer the Reformation's complaint with an inventory. An inventory is not an answer. The model congregation reaches the text itself, “searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11), and the apostolic charge exists for a people's sake, “give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13), not a shelf's.

pos: n. (the Luxembourg abbey founded 698 by Willibrord, missionary to the Frisians)
etymology: From Latin Epternacum, of uncertain origin; the German spelling has prevailed.
biblical_def: Echternach on the Sure in what is now Luxembourg was founded in 698 by Willibrord, the Northumbrian monk trained at Ripon and in Ireland who spent some forty years preaching among the Frisians as archbishop of Utrecht. He made Echternach his base and was buried there in 739; the abbey became a major scriptorium, producing the Echternach Gospels and the Codex Aureus, and it preserved the calendar in which Willibrord's own hand noted the year of his arrival. The dancing procession held at Echternach at Whitsun is among the oldest continuous religious processions in Europe. The dictionary records Echternach for Willibrord, the second great figure of the Anglo-Saxon mission after Boniface, and for the plain fact that the conversion of the Low Countries was done by men who went. “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Mat 28:19) is the commission as it stands, “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) the method, and “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11) the confidence that sent a Yorkshireman to the Frisian coast for four decades.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a scriptorium is given under scribe as a writer; a missionary as one sent to propagate religion; a procession as a train of persons walking in order; a calendar as a register of the year; and Whitsuntide as the feast of Pentecost.
webster_full: SCRIBE, n. A writer; a notary; a public writer; in Scripture, a clerk or secretary.
MISSIONARY, n. One sent to propagate religion; a person sent by ecclesiastical authority to preach the gospel.
PROCESSION, n. The act of proceeding or issuing forth; a train of persons walking or riding in ceremonious solemnity.
CALENDAR, n. A register of the year, with its divisions; an almanack.
WHITSUNTIDE, n. The feast of Pentecost; a festival of the church held in commemoration of the descent of the Holy Spirit.
scriptures: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
corruption_summary: Luxembourg abbey founded 698 by Willibrord, apostle of the Frisians, a major scriptorium and his burial place.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that somebody has to go. Willibrord left Northumbria for the Frisian coast and stayed forty years, and the commission he obeyed has no qualifying clause: “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Mat 28:19). The method was not complicated, “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2).

The live temptation is to credit the result to the abbey and the scriptorium that followed. They followed; they did not cause. The mechanism is Paul's, “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17), and the confidence that makes a four-decade mission rational is Isaiah's, “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11).
